### Reproducible Presentation Workflow

The professor also went over a sample Case 31 presentation and explained how we can follow a similar process for our own work. The presentation is created from a source file that includes the slide content, R code, analysis results, and visualizations. This means we don't have to manually recreate every slide whenever something in our analysis changes.

The basic workflow looks like this:

1. Keep our dataset, analysis code, and presentation source file together in the project folder.
2. Write our analysis and create the visualizations directly in the QMD file.
3. Use code chunks to run calculations and generate tables or graphs.
4. Render the QMD file using the `revealjs` format.
5. Whenever we update the code or content, we can render the file again to generate an updated HTML presentation.

One of the biggest benefits of this approach is that everything stays connected. If we need to fix something in our data preparation, change a variable, run a different statistical test, or adjust a graph, we can simply update the source file and render it again. The presentation will then reflect those changes without us having to manually update each slide.

The professor emphasized that we should follow the **workflow and structure of the sample**, rather than just copying the finished HTML presentation. Each group still needs to use its own Case 31 data, variables, research questions, results, and interpretations.

The sample presentation also gives us a good idea of how to organize our work. It starts with the case background and research questions, then moves into the methods, data preparation, sample characteristics, measures, analysis, results, and insights.

The analysis is organized by research question and the type of statistical test being used. Some of the methods shown include:

- One-sample and two-sample t-tests.
- Chi-square tests for independence and goodness of fit.
- ANOVA and ANCOVA.
- MANOVA.
- Multiple regression.

# Module Reference: Chapter 16 (Not Covered in Class)

The following information comes from our module notes. I'm including it as a reference for Chapter 16 since the material was mentioned but wasn't actually covered during this class session.

# Descriptive Statistics

## Meaning and Purpose

Descriptive statistics help us summarize and understand the information in our dataset. They're usually one of the first things we look at because they give us a better idea of what we've collected, how the responses are distributed, and whether there are any issues we should address before moving into hypothesis testing.

We can use descriptive statistics to look at individual variables or explore how different variables relate to one another.

For example:

- **Frequency distributions** help us understand how responses are spread across the different values or categories of a single variable.
- **Cross-tabulations** allow us to compare how one variable is distributed across the categories of another variable.

One thing to remember is that descriptive statistics alone don't prove whether a hypothesis is true. Instead, they help us organize the information, recognize patterns, and decide which statistical tests make the most sense for our research questions.

## Frequency Distributions

A frequency distribution shows us how many observations fall into each category or value of a variable. The frequency count is simply the number of times a particular response or value appears in the dataset.

We can also look at percentages and valid percentages to better understand how the responses compare. This is especially helpful when we're comparing groups that don't have the same number of observations.

When reviewing a frequency distribution, I should pay attention to:

- The different categories or values in the variable.
- How many observations fall into each category.
- What percentage of the total each category represents.
- The total number of valid responses.
- Whether there are any missing values or unusual responses.

Frequency distributions are especially useful when working with categorical variables, such as gender, education level, or yes/no questions.

We can also use them with numerical variables, particularly when the individual values or ranges tell us something meaningful about the data.

## Measures of Location

Measures of location help us understand where the center of our data is. In other words, they give us an idea of what a typical value looks like within a distribution.

The three main measures we'll be looking at are the mean, median, and mode.

### Mean

The **mean** is what we typically think of as the average. We calculate it by adding up all the values and dividing by the total number of observations.

The mean is useful when averaging makes sense for the type of data we're working with. However, one thing to keep in mind is that unusually high or low values can pull the average in one direction.

For example, if most respondents have relatively similar incomes but one person has an extremely high income, that single response could raise the mean quite a bit.

### Median

The **median** is the middle value when all our observations are arranged from lowest to highest.

If we split the data at the median, approximately half of the observations fall below it and half fall above it.

One advantage of the median is that it isn't affected as much by extreme values. This can make it more useful than the mean when our data is skewed or contains outliers.

For example, when looking at income data, the median might give us a better idea of what a typical respondent earns if a few people have much higher incomes than everyone else.

### Mode

The **mode** is the value or category that appears most frequently in our dataset.

This is especially useful when working with nominal variables because those categories don't necessarily have a numerical order.

For example, if we're looking at respondents' preferred shopping methods, the mode would tell us which option was selected the most.

The main thing to remember is that **we shouldn't automatically use the mean for every variable just because our statistical software provides it**.

We need to consider the type of variable, its measurement scale, and how the values are distributed before deciding which measure gives us the most useful information.


## Measures of Variability

Measures of variability help us understand how spread out the values are in our dataset. While measures of location tell us where the center of the data is, measures of variability show us how much the individual observations differ from one another.

### Range

The **range** is the difference between the highest and lowest values in our dataset.

It's one of the easiest ways to understand how spread out our data is, but it does have a limitation. Since it only looks at the two extreme values, it doesn't tell us much about how the rest of the observations are distributed.

For example, if most respondents have similar incomes but one person earns significantly more than everyone else, that one response could make the range much larger.

### Variance

**Variance** measures how much our observations differ from the mean by looking at their average squared distance from it.

Essentially, it gives us an idea of how much variation exists within the dataset.

One thing to keep in mind is that variance uses squared units. This can make the results harder to interpret directly, especially when we're working with measurements like income, age, or other numerical variables.

### Standard Deviation

The **standard deviation** is the square root of the variance. It's usually easier to interpret because it's expressed in the same units as the original variable.

It helps us understand how closely the observations are grouped around the mean.

- **Smaller standard deviation:** The values are more closely grouped around the mean, meaning there's less variation in the data.
- **Larger standard deviation:** The values are more spread out from the mean, meaning there's more variation between observations.

For example, if we're comparing customer spending between two groups, they could have the same average spending but very different standard deviations. One group might spend relatively similar amounts, while the other has customers spending both very little and quite a lot.

The important thing to remember is that **measures of location and variability should be looked at together**.

Knowing the mean is helpful, but it doesn't tell us how consistent the observations are. We also need to understand how much the values vary to get a better picture of what's happening in our data.

# Cross-Tabulation

## Purpose of a Cross-Tabulation

A **cross-tabulation**, also called a cross-tab, is a table that allows us to compare two categorical variables at the same time.

Instead of looking at each variable separately, we can use a cross-tab to see how the responses for one variable are distributed across the categories of another.

Typically, we're comparing a **dependent variable** against an **independent variable** to see whether there's a pattern or possible relationship between them.

For example, if we're studying whether people are interested in joining a credit union, we could compare their responses across different demographic or behavioral groups.

The cross-tab would allow us to see how many people in each group said they were interested, along with the percentages for each category.

Cross-tabulation works best with categorical variables, including:

- **Nominal variables:** Categories that don't have a natural order, such as gender or preferred banking institution.
- **Ordinal variables:** Categories that have a meaningful order, such as satisfaction levels or education categories.

One thing to remember is that a cross-tab helps us **identify possible associations between variables**, but the table alone doesn't tell us whether those patterns are statistically significant.

To determine whether the differences we're seeing are likely to be more than random variation, we need to use an appropriate statistical test, such as the chi-square test of independence.

This is why cross-tabulation is useful during our analysis. It gives us a way to visually compare groups and recognize patterns before testing whether those relationships are statistically significant.


## Rows and Columns

When creating a cross-tabulation, we generally place the **independent variable in the columns** and the **dependent variable in the rows**.

This makes it easier to compare how the dependent variable changes across the different categories of the independent variable.

However, the most important thing isn't necessarily where we place the variables. What really matters is that we're calculating and interpreting the percentages in a way that actually answers our research question.

For example, if we're trying to understand how interest in joining a credit union differs between age groups, we would want to look at the percentage of interested respondents within each age group.

When reviewing a cross-tab, I should make sure I understand:

- Which variable is independent and which is dependent.
- What the numbers in each cell actually represent.
- Whether we're looking at row percentages or column percentages.
- Whether the differences between groups are large enough to be meaningful.
- Whether a statistical test supports the relationship we're seeing.

The main takeaway is that **we need to pay attention to how we're reading the percentages**, not just the numbers in the table. Otherwise, we could end up interpreting the relationship incorrectly.

## Observed and Expected Counts

When working with cross-tabulations and chi-square tests, we need to understand the difference between **observed counts** and **expected counts**.

- **Observed counts:** The actual number of responses or observations that fall into each cell of our table.
- **Expected counts:** The number of observations we would expect to see in each cell if there were no relationship between the two variables, based on the row and column totals.

By comparing the observed and expected counts, we can start to see where differences or possible relationships might exist.

If the observed counts are very different from what we expected, those differences can contribute to a larger chi-square statistic.

However, we can't automatically assume that a large difference means there's a statistically significant relationship. We still need to look at the results of the overall test and consider what those differences mean in the context of our research.

# Hypothesis Testing

## General Process

Hypothesis testing gives us a structured way to evaluate a claim about a population using data collected from a sample.

Instead of making assumptions based on what we see in the data, we use statistical tests to determine whether there's enough evidence to support a particular conclusion.

The general process looks like this:

1. **Identify the research question:** Determine what we're trying to find out and establish our null and alternative hypotheses.
2. **Choose the appropriate statistical test:** Select a test based on the variables we're analyzing and the type of research we're conducting.
3. **Set the significance level:** Decide what level of statistical significance we'll use before evaluating the results.
4. **Run the analysis:** Calculate the test statistic and obtain the p-value.
5. **Compare the results:** Look at whether the p-value is smaller than our selected significance level.
6. **Make a decision:** Determine whether we should reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis.
7. **Interpret the findings:** Explain what the results mean in plain language and connect them back to our research question.

There are two main hypotheses we need to understand:

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** Generally assumes there's no difference, no relationship, or no meaningful departure from an expected distribution.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1):** Suggests that a difference, relationship, or departure from the expected distribution does exist.

One important thing to remember is that **statistical significance doesn't automatically mean something is practically important**.

A statistically significant result tells us that the observed data would be relatively unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, based on the significance level we selected.

However, it doesn't necessarily tell us why the relationship exists, whether one variable causes another, or whether the difference is large enough to matter in a real-world situation.

## Significance and Interpretation

When interpreting a hypothesis test, we compare the **p-value** to the significance level we selected, which is commonly 0.05.

The basic rule is:

- **If p < 0.05:** We reject the null hypothesis because the results are statistically significant at the 5% level.
- **If p >= 0.05:** We fail to reject the null hypothesis because we don't have enough statistical evidence to conclude that a difference or relationship exists at that level.

This assumes we've chosen a significance level of 0.05. If we're using a different significance level, we would compare the p-value to that instead.

Something the professor wants us to understand is that **failing to reject the null hypothesis doesn't mean we've proven it to be true**.

It simply means our analysis didn't provide enough evidence to reject it.

We also need to remember that statistical significance is only one part of interpreting our results.

When explaining our findings, we should also consider:

- The size of our sample.
- How strong the relationship or difference appears to be.
- Whether the variables were measured appropriately.
- Whether the findings actually help answer our research question.

The goal isn't just to report a p-value. We need to explain what the results tell us and why they matter.

# Chi-Square Tests

## Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test

The **chi-square goodness-of-fit test** is used when we're analyzing a single categorical variable.

It allows us to compare the number of observations we actually collected with the number we would expect to see based on a particular distribution.

For example, imagine we're surveying customers about their preferred shopping method. We might want to test whether customers are equally likely to prefer shopping online, in-store, or through a mobile app.

If we expect each option to receive an equal percentage of responses, we can compare that expectation against the actual results of our survey.

The expected distribution doesn't always have to be equal. It can also be based on specific percentages established by our research question or previous information.

The test helps us determine whether the differences between the observed and expected frequencies are statistically significant.

The main thing to remember is that **the goodness-of-fit test only looks at one categorical variable**.

We're testing whether its distribution matches what we expected, not whether two different variables are related.

## Chi-Square Test of Independence

The **chi-square test of independence** is used when we want to determine whether there's a relationship between two categorical variables.

This test builds on cross-tabulation because we're comparing the actual counts in each cell of the table with the counts we would expect if the variables were unrelated.

For example, we might want to know whether a customer's age group is associated with their preferred shopping method.

We could create a cross-tabulation comparing age groups with shopping preferences and then use the chi-square test of independence to see whether the differences are statistically significant.

For this test, our hypotheses would be:

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** The two variables are independent, meaning there's no association between them in the population.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1):** The two variables are associated, meaning there is a relationship between them in the population.

If our results are statistically significant, we have evidence that the two variables are associated.

However, **an association doesn't necessarily mean that one variable causes the other**.

For example, even if age group and shopping preference are statistically associated, that doesn't automatically mean age itself is the reason someone prefers a particular shopping method.

There could be other factors influencing that relationship.

The biggest difference between the two chi-square tests is what we're trying to analyze:

- **Goodness-of-fit:** Looks at one categorical variable and compares its observed distribution with an expected distribution.
- **Test of independence:** Looks at two categorical variables and tests whether there's an association between them.

Understanding this difference will help us choose the correct test when working through our Case 31 research questions in R.


## Conditions and Cautions

When using chi-square tests, we need to make sure we're working with categorical variables and that our expected cell counts are large enough for the test to be reliable.

If some categories have very few responses, the chi-square approximation might not be accurate. This is why it's important to check the expected counts before interpreting our results.

If we run into categories with very small counts, we may need to combine some of them. However, we shouldn't combine categories just to make the test work. There needs to be a logical reason for grouping them together based on what we're studying.

Another important thing to remember is that **reporting a p-value by itself isn't enough**.

We also need to explain what the cross-tabulation is showing us, including how the percentages differ between groups and what those differences mean for our research question.

# Adding a Third Variable

## Purpose

A cross-tabulation with two variables can help us identify a possible relationship, but sometimes there's more going on than what we see in the original table.

By introducing a **third variable**, we can take a closer look at that relationship and see whether it stays consistent across different groups.

For example, we might find an overall relationship between age and shopping preferences. However, when we separate respondents by income level, we could discover that the relationship is much stronger for certain income groups than others.

Adding a third variable can help us understand whether:

- The original relationship stays about the same across different groups.
- The relationship becomes weaker or disappears.
- The relationship only exists for certain groups.
- The relationship changes in strength or direction depending on the group.

The main reason for doing this is that **the overall relationship doesn't always tell us the full story**.

Looking at additional variables can help us better understand what's actually happening in our data.

## Four Possible Patterns

According to the module, there are four main patterns we might see when adding a third variable to our analysis.

1. **Replication:** The relationship we originally observed continues to appear across the different subgroups. In other words, adding the third variable doesn't really change the pattern we were seeing.

2. **Explanation:** The original relationship becomes weaker or disappears after we account for the third variable. This suggests that the third variable might help explain why we saw the relationship in the first place.

3. **Specification:** The relationship only appears within certain categories of the third variable. This helps us identify which groups are actually showing the association.

4. **Interpretation or Interaction:** The strength or direction of the relationship changes depending on the subgroup. This means we may need to interpret the relationship differently for different groups instead of treating everyone the same.

When interpreting these patterns, we should look closely at the percentages within each subgroup and consider how they relate to our research question.

We also shouldn't add a third variable just because we have more data available. **There should be a research-based reason for including it**, whether that's something supported by theory or something that makes sense in the context of our study.

# Using R for Cross-Tabulation and Chi-Square Analysis

## General Workflow

When performing cross-tabulation and chi-square analysis in R, we're following the same general process we learned conceptually. The difference is that we're using R to organize the data, calculate the results, and run our statistical tests.

The general workflow looks like this:

1. **Load our data and packages:** Start by importing the dataset and loading any R packages we need.
2. **Review the variables:** Check the variables we're working with and make sure we understand how they're coded.
3. **Check variable types and missing values:** Confirm that we're using categorical variables and that missing responses are handled appropriately.
4. **Create frequency tables:** Look at the distribution of responses for each variable individually.
5. **Create the cross-tabulation:** Compare the independent and dependent variables in a table.
6. **Calculate the percentages:** Make sure we're using row or column percentages that actually answer our research question.
7. **Run the chi-square test:** Use the appropriate test to determine whether the observed differences are statistically significant.
8. **Review the output:** Check the expected counts, test statistic, and p-value.
9. **Interpret the findings:** Explain what the results mean and how they relate to our research question.

One thing to remember is that **just because our R code runs without errors doesn't mean our analysis is correct**.

We still need to make sure the variables are coded properly, the table is organized correctly, and the statistical test is appropriate for what we're trying to answer.

## Example R Structure

The exact variable names will depend on the dataset we're using, but we can organize our analysis with functions like these:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Frequency counts
table(data$variable)

# Cross-tabulation
tab <- table(data$dependent_variable, data$independent_variable)
tab

# Row or column proportions
prop.table(tab, margin = 1)
prop.table(tab, margin = 2)

# Chi-square test of independence
chisq.test(tab)
```

The `margin` argument tells R which direction to use when calculating percentages.

- **margin = 1:** Calculates percentages within each row.
- **margin = 2:** Calculates percentages within each column.

Since we're generally placing our dependent variable in the rows and independent variable in the columns, we would typically use `margin = 2` when comparing responses across the independent-variable groups.

However, we should always double-check that the percentages we're calculating match what our research question is asking.

For a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, we can also specify the expected probabilities when the categories aren't supposed to have equal proportions.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Goodness-of-fit example structure
observed <- table(data$categorical_variable)
chisq.test(observed, p = c(0.25, 0.25, 0.50))
```

In this example, we're testing an expected distribution of 25%, 25%, and 50% across three categories.

These examples are meant to show us how the R commands are structured. When working with our actual dataset, we'll need to use the correct variable names, expected probabilities, and interpretations based on the research question.

# Connecting the Analysis to the Data Analysis Table

The **data analysis table** is important because it helps us connect our analytics objectives to the specific variables and statistical tests we'll be using.

Instead of just deciding to run different analyses, we're creating a plan that explains what we're trying to answer and how we're going to answer it.

Each analytics objective can be broken down into smaller research questions or hypotheses, which makes the analysis more manageable.

Our data analysis table should include:

- **Construct:** The concept or characteristic we're trying to study.
- **Research question or hypothesis:** What we're specifically trying to find out or test.
- **Question or variable:** The survey question or dataset variable we're using to measure the construct.
- **Scale of measurement:** Whether the variable is nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio.
- **Type of analysis:** The general approach we'll use to analyze the data.
- **Statistical technique:** The specific test or method we'll use to answer the research question.

One thing we need to pay attention to is the **scale of measurement**, since this helps determine which statistical methods are appropriate.

The four measurement scales are:

- **Nominal:** Categories without a natural order, such as preferred shopping method or gender.
- **Ordinal:** Categories with a meaningful order, such as satisfaction levels.
- **Interval:** Numerical values with equal distances between them, but without a true zero point.
- **Ratio:** Numerical values with equal distances and a meaningful zero point, such as age or income.

For example, if we're working with nominal variables, we can count how many observations fall into each category.

If we're working with interval or ratio variables, we may be able to calculate statistics like the mean, depending on the assumptions and what we're trying to measure.

It's also important to understand the difference between our **constructs-and-measures table** and our **data analysis table**.

The constructs-and-measures table focuses on defining the concepts we're studying and explaining how we're measuring them.

The data analysis table takes that a step further by showing how we'll actually use those measurements to answer our research questions.

Basically, one table explains **what we're measuring**, while the other explains **how we're going to analyze it**.

# Class Activities and Takeaways

## Module Planning Activity

For the module planning activity, we're supposed to look through all the steps before starting the actual work.

The goal is to get a better idea of how much time the assignment will take and make sure we're not leaving everything until the last minute.

The activity asks us to:

- Review all the steps involved in the module.
- Estimate how much time we'll need to complete each part.
- Identify any important deadlines.
- Set aside at least twice the amount of time we originally estimated.

The idea behind doubling our estimated time is to give ourselves some flexibility in case we run into problems with the data, R code, or analysis.

This is especially useful for assignments like Case 31, where we might need to troubleshoot our code, review our variables, or rerun analyses before everything is ready.

Planning ahead should make it easier to manage the assignment and give us enough time to actually understand the results instead of just rushing to finish the work.
